title: Beef Enchiladas
subtitle: Spiced beef mince rolled in corn tortillas with a deep red chilli sauce
excerpt: Corn tortillas filled with spiced beef mince, rolled and baked under a rich red chilli sauce and a blanket of melted cheese. A Tex-Mex classic that improves when made ahead.
sourceNotes: Beef enchiladas: a core Tex-Mex dish derived from Mexican enchiladas, simplified for the US home pantry. The red chilli sauce is adapted from dried chilli-based Mexican sauces. Drawn from classic American Tex-Mex home-cooking sources and Rosarita brand-influenced 1950s American cookbook traditions.

recipe.freezeNotes: Assemble, cover tightly, and freeze before baking for up to 3 months. Add 15 minutes to the bake time from frozen.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a double batch; freeze one unbaked tray for a future meal.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble up to a day ahead and refrigerate unbaked. Bring to room temperature before the oven.

glossaryTerms.definition: A corn tortilla filled and rolled, then baked under a chilli sauce and melted cheese. The name comes from the Spanish word for 'chilli-seasoned'.

content.text: are corn tortillas stuffed with spiced beef, rolled, and baked under a red chilli sauce thick enough to coat a spoon. The tortillas soften as they bake; the cheese on top crisps at the edges. This is the Tex-Mex version: saucier and cheesier than the Mexican original, and built for the oven rather than a griddle.

items.prepNote: soaked in boiling water 20 minutes, drained
add if not using ancho chilli

content.text: A roasting dish that holds 8 tortillas side by side is the right vessel; a standard 30 cm × 20 cm dish works. The corn tortillas need a brief dip in the warm red sauce before rolling so they stay pliable and don't crack.
Heat {{vegetable-oil}} of oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook {{onion}} finely chopped onion for 5 minutes. Add {{garlic}} of crushed garlic and cook for 1 minute.
Add {{beef-mince}} of beef mince. Break up and cook for 5-6 minutes until browned. Stir in the chilli powder and cumin, season with salt, and cook for 2 minutes. Set aside.

Blend the tinned tomatoes, soaked ancho chillies (or extra chilli powder), garlic, and cumin together until smooth. Pour into a saucepan with {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock. Simmer for 10 minutes until slightly thickened. Season with salt. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon.
Heat the oven to 190°C. Spread a ladleful of red sauce across the base of the roasting dish.

Dip each corn tortilla into the warm red sauce for 10 seconds; it softens enough to roll without cracking. Lay flat, add 2-3 tablespoons of beef filling, and scatter over a little cheese. Roll tightly and place seam-side down in the dish. Repeat with the remaining tortillas.

Pour the remaining red sauce over the enchiladas. Top with the rest of the grated cheese. Bake at 190°C for 20-25 minutes until the cheese is bubbling and lightly browned at the edges. Rest for 5 minutes before serving.
Spoon soured cream over the top and scatter with coriander.

items.cause: Corn tortillas not warmed or dipped in sauce before rolling
items.fix: Dip each tortilla in the warm red sauce for 10 seconds before filling. The heat and moisture makes them pliable.

items.symptom: The sauce is too thin and watery
items.cause: Not enough cooking time to reduce
items.fix: Simmer the sauce for longer before assembling. It should coat a spoon; thin sauce will make the dish soggy.

items.symptom: Cheese goes rubbery rather than melting
items.cause: Oven temperature too low, or low-moisture pre-grated cheese used
items.fix: Use freshly grated cheddar rather than bags of pre-grated; the anti-caking starch in pre-grated cheese prevents proper melting. Keep the oven at 190°C.

items.cause: Tortillas overfilled, or rolled too loosely
items.fix: Use 2-3 tablespoons of filling per tortilla. Roll firmly and place seam-side down so the weight of the sauce holds them closed.

content.text: Enchiladas are one of Mexico's oldest recorded dishes. Corn tortillas dipped in chilli sauce appear in Spanish accounts of Aztec markets. The Tex-Mex version uses a ground beef filling with a heavy cheese topping. It grew through the 20th century in Mexican-American communities and spread into mainstream US homes from there. Enchiladas bake, reheat, and freeze so well that they've become a staple of home freezer cooking.
